https://www.ksl.com:443/article/51611867.text: IDAHO FALLS — Averaging nearly 150 homes per day, riding his bike up and down neighborhoods, a foreign college student is selling books to help fund his educational journey, thousands of miles away from home.While many in the community may have already interacted with him, his name is Kert Raudnomm, 22, from Voru, Estonia, who has been in Idaho Falls since June.Raudnomm is selling educational books from Southwestern Advantage, and this is his third year selling those materials to Americans. He told EastIdahoNews.com that he's been selling these books to fund his studies at a university in Tallinn, Estonia's capital.Southwestern Advantage is a sales and leadership program that allows college or university students to sell educational materials while developing entrepreneurial skills. The educational materials range from preschool, all the way up to high school classes.He is currently pursuing a master's degree after graduating with a bachelor's in economics and business management.What brought him around the globe was the chance to leave his home country, experience America, and make money on the side."I really like that I can like knock on a door and see like real people because in like Hollywood movies, it doesn't reflect like the real America," Raudnomm said.During his door-to-door route, Raudnomm said one of his more unique experiences was running into members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints who've served missions in his home country.He said this experience allowed him to speak Estonian, and he was surprised that those individuals still speak that language.While Idaho has been his most recent stop, Raudnomm spent previous summers in the Mountain West, living in Logan and Salt Lake City, Utah.With these experiences, Raudnomm said his hometown has a population of 10,000, and that has changed how he views things when he's back in Estonia. The European nation is relatively small, with a population of only 1.36 million — fewer than Idaho's population."I'm more confident in connecting with people and also have better habits as well," Raudnomm said.He's only here for the summer, though. Raudnomm's time is short, and he will be making his way back home at the end of August. Once there, he will continue his studies at Tallinn University.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Authorities found four deceased victims in a home in Houma, Louisiana. Photograph: Rawf8/Alamy View image in fullscreen Authorities found four deceased victims in a home in Houma, Louisiana. Photograph: Rawf8/Alamy Louisiana Four dead in Louisiana stabbing spree as police arrest person of interest Kaegan Jude Solet, 47, taken into custody after stabbings in Houma leave four dead and one wounded, authorities say Keely Aouga Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.34 EDT First published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police arrested a person of interest after a series of stabbings in Houma, Louisiana , left at least four people dead and another person in critical condition in hospital. The Terrebonne parish sheriff’s office confirmed Kaegan Jude Solet, 47, had been taken into custody after deputies were initially called to the Ashland Drive area of Houma and located a juvenile with apparent stab wounds. “This remains an active and ongoing investigation. Additional information will be released as soon as it becomes available,” the office said in a statement. The victim was airlifted to an out-of-area hospital and remains in critical condition. As the investigation continued, authorities later found four deceased victims in a nearby home. Solet was previously arrested in connection with a 2019 stabbing in Houma. According to a Houma police department news release, Solet, then 40, was accused of repeatedly stabbing a 59-year-old woman at a hotel following an argument. Solet was identified as a suspect in the case when investigators learned he was a guest in the victim’s room. Officers said the pair had got into some kind of argument and Solet stabbed the victim repeatedly in the upper body and head. She was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries. Solet was booked at the time on one count of attempted second-degree murder. The 2019 case is separate from the current investigation. The identification of a person of interest does not constitute an arrest or criminal charge. Authorities have not announced any charges against him in the current case. The current investigation remains ongoing as detectives continue gathering evidence and developing information surrounding the incidents. https://www.politico.eu/article/dutch-op.text: The largest opposition party in the Netherlands has chosen to join the European Socialists rather than the Greens in an internal vote, the results of which were announced Friday. Some 65% of votes cast by members of Progressive Netherlands (PRO), which was formed earlier this year when the Dutch GreenLeft (GroenLinks) and Labour (PvdA) parties merged, backed joining the Party of European Socialists instead of the European Green Party. Before voting began, an advisory committee to the party recommended joining the PES, arguing that membership would give the party greater influence at the European level. Advertisement Advertisement “There are only three European political families represented at all three levels [of the EU],” the advisory committee wrote in a report, adding that the PES has “prime ministers, the President of the European Council, European Commissioners, and leaders of national parties.” “The Greens … have fewer ministers, no members of the European Commission, and no heads of government; consequently, their preliminary consultations carry less weight,” the report went on. PRO leader Jesse Klaver joined a PES meeting ahead of the European Council summit in June, alongside Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen. What about the MEPs? European political parties and political groups in the European Parliament are closely linked, but they are not the same thing. A PRO spokesperson told POLITICO that the party’s eight MEPs are likely to remain in their current parliamentary groups: four in the Socialists and Democrats and four in the Greens/European Free Alliance. The spokesperson said PRO would likely review the arrangement ahead of the next European Parliament election in 2029. Advertisement Advertisement The choice of European party will, however, have implications for the allocation of EU funding. Most EU cash for European political parties is distributed according to their share of MEPs. Under the rules, the PES could count all eight PRO MEPs toward its funding share, even if four remain in the Greens. The Dutch party told POLITICO one option would be for the four MEPs from the former GroenLinks side to technically leave PRO, allowing them to be counted separately under the funding rules.

https://bnn-news.com/bnn-in-focus/bnn-in.text: Photo: LETA/BNN collage/AI Advertisements The success of the decision to join forces was already demonstrated by Sovereign Power/Young Latvians (SV/J) in the Riga municipal election, where the alliance won eight seats. Shortly before the 15th Saeima election, it appears that this success could be repeated. That does not, however, mean that SV/J could enter government. It can be said with near certainty that, just as in Riga City Council, the alliance would find itself in opposition in parliament as well. Fierce competition for the protest vote A poll conducted by Latvijas Fakti in cooperation with Faktu logs showed support for the alliance at 6.3% in August and 5.9% in September. However, the 0.4 percentage-point decline does not yet provide grounds to conclude that SV/J is experiencing a sustained fall in popularity. Rather, it suggests that competition for protest-minded and Russian-speaking voters is becoming increasingly intense. This segment is already crowded, while SV/J is simultaneously competing across several political territories: with Stability! for protest-minded and Russian-speaking voters; with Harmony Centre and the Latvian Russian Union (LKS) for the traditional ethnic-minority electorate; with Gobzems’ List for voters shaped by the Covid-era protests and more radical anti-establishment sentiment; and with Latvia First (LPV) for socially conservative voters opposed to the government’s course, as well as part of the Russian-speaking electorate. Advertisements One of the cornerstones of SV/J’s success is precisely its ability to bring together these different political groups and appeal to the broadest possible spectrum of protest voters. This includes the “everything is bad” voter, part of the Russian-speaking electorate, the Covid-era protest audience, socially conservative voters and those who disagree with Latvia’s current policies on Ukraine and defence. Another factor is the 20% of respondents who remain undecided and the 12.9% who say they do not intend to vote. This leaves a relatively large pool of people whose dissatisfaction has not yet translated into support for a particular party – and this is the “pond” in which political forces can still fish for a sizeable catch. SV/J’s election promises Advertisements SV/J’s official objectives include reviewing the terms of Latvia’s membership in supranational organisations, keeping strategic state-owned companies under state control and protecting traditional values. Its election programme proposes a popularly elected president, reducing the Saeima to 50 MPs, downsizing the public administration, abolishing the State Defence Service, reallocating defence funding, assessing Latvia’s possible withdrawal from the World Health Organization, preserving the use of cash, opposing digital currency, and expanding the use of referendums and citizens’ opportunities to influence state decisions. SV/J promises to set the minimum pension at no less than half the minimum wage, raise the state family allowance to one-quarter of the minimum wage for each child, increase the tax-free minimum to the level of the minimum wage and allow people to withdraw their second-pillar pension savings. At the same time, the programme includes a range of tax cuts. Voters are therefore being offered a highly attractive package: lower taxes combined with greater social support. A separate question is whether these promises are fiscally feasible at all. Advertisements The programme also proposes allowing private schools to teach in minority languages and giving schools the option of restoring Russian-language instruction. SV/J leader Jūlija Stepaņenko has also spoken in favour of simplifying the process by which non-citizens can obtain Latvian citizenship. This is the “carrot” that may persuade a considerable number of voters to support SV/J. Pensioners may be drawn to the promise of a higher minimum pension; families to larger child benefits; entrepreneurs to lower taxes and less bureaucracy; Russian-speaking voters to proposals concerning the Russian language and citizenship for non-citizens; socially conservative voters to the emphasis on family values; opponents of Covid-era restrictions to scepticism towards the WHO and state institutions; opponents of the State Defence Service to the promise of abolishing compulsory service; and voters who disagree with Latvia’s current Ukraine policy to the proposal to stop financing military support for Ukraine. Once again, however, it is worth remembering that election promises – regardless of which party makes them – should be viewed critically, including by asking whether a single political force would actually be able to implement them. Party figures and reputational problems Advertisements Young Latvians was founded in 2023 by Rūdolfs Brēmanis, Edgars Dārznieks and Artūrs Klēbahs, former members of Aldis Gobzems’ For Each and Every party. Gobzems himself ran on the Young Latvians list in the 2024 European Parliament election. Jūlija Stepaņenko was originally elected to the Saeima from the Harmony list. During the pandemic, she was among the MPs unable to participate in the work of the Saeima because of the Covid-19 certificate requirement and challenged the restriction before the Constitutional Court. The Covid-sceptical political environment and active campaigning on social media may be among the factors behind Sovereign Power’s popularity. The party itself, however, has a much longer history. The Union – Heart of Latgale party, registered in 2005, was renamed Law. Responsibility. Order in 2019 and became Sovereign Power in July 2022. Jūlija Stepaņenko joined the party at that time and became chair of its board, taking over the position from her husband, Vjačeslavs Stepaņenko. Advertisements Jūlija Stepaņenko is the alliance’s central political figure and its candidate for prime minister. Her advantages include extensive parliamentary experience and very high name recognition. Her political biography, however, also shows movement between several political forces: Harmony, Honor to Serve Riga (GKR), Latvia First and, subsequently, Sovereign Power. In 2022, Latvia First expelled Stepaņenko and Ļubova Švecova after they did not join the party’s condemnation of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine. An even more notable issue concerns the two gifts – cash and an apartment – worth a combined 419,598 euros that Jūlija Stepaņenko received from her father, Sergei Fedotov, who lives in Russia. The Insider established that Fedotov owns 72.68% of Forma ZhBI and 73.45% of PLK Forma, companies that have provided specific support to Russia’s military infrastructure. Advertisements If a candidate for prime minister has received very substantial material support from a close relative in Russia whose company has also supplied fortifications for the needs of the Russian army, questions inevitably arise about the nature of these financial ties, the origin of the money and the possibility of influence by a foreign state. It remains to be seen what Latvia’s security authorities will say about the matter. Rūdolfs Brēmanis carries an even heavier burden in terms of political reputation. He has been charged in criminal proceedings over the alleged fraudulent acquisition of approximately 102,721 euros while working in Latvia’s diplomatic service in the United Arab Emirates. The case is currently being heard by Riga City Court. Following the 2024 European Parliament election, a court also ordered him to delete claims circulated on social media alleging that the election results had been falsified. Specifically, Brēmanis had posted videos on Facebook and TikTok in which he claimed that, “according to unofficial information, the Central Election Commission would most likely falsify the votes that had been cast for safekeeping.” Advertisements Does this mean that the scandals surrounding the party’s leaders will cause at least some SV/J supporters to turn away from the alliance? Probably not. While such a history of conflicts may reduce trust in a protest party among one group of voters, another may interpret politicians’ clashes with state institutions as evidence that they stand outside the “system”.
